title: Capitalization
description: R&E capitalization under IRC Section 174 requires U.S. taxpayers to capitalize research and experimental expenditures rather than deduct them immediately.
summary: R&E capitalization under IRC Section 174 requires U.S. taxpayers to capitalize research and experimental expenditures rather than deduct them immediately. For 2022–2024, domestic costs were amortized over five years and foreign costs over 15 years. Starting in 2025, Section 174A restores immediate expensing for domestic research, while foreign research remains subject to mandatory 15-year amortization.

body.text: R&E capitalization under IRC Section 174 requires U.S. taxpayers to capitalize research and experimental expenditures rather than deduct them immediately. For 2022–2024, domestic costs were amortized over five years and foreign costs over 15 years. Starting in 2025, Section 174A restores immediate expensing for domestic research, while foreign research remains subject to mandatory 15-year amortization.
Executive Summary and Statutory Mandate

Within the framework of United States federal income tax law, capitalization under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 174 mandates that companies cannot immediately deduct specified research or experimental (SRE) expenditures in the taxable year in which those costs are paid or incurred when governed by the statutory amortization regime. Enacted originally as Section 13206(a) of the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA, Public Law 115-97, 131 Stat. 2054, December 22, 2017) and taking effect for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, this statutory revision eliminated the longstanding pre-2022 election to immediately expense research and development (R&D) outlays. Instead, for all taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, taxpayers were legally compelled to treat all qualifying domestic and foreign SRE expenditures as capital investments recorded on the tax balance sheet and recover those costs systematically through multi-year amortization. Under the TCJA post-2021 statutory regime, capitalized SRE expenditures attributable to domestic research activities conducted within the United States had to be amortized ratably over a five-year (60-month) period, whereas expenditures attributable to foreign research activities conducted outside the United States had to be amortized over a fifteen-year (180-month) period. In both jurisdictions, cost recovery must commence at the midpoint of the taxable year in which the expenditures are paid or incurred, utilizing a mandatory mid-year convention.

Subsequently, on July 4, 2025, the enactment of Section 70302 of the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, Public Law 119-21, 139 Stat. 72) established a permanently bifurcated statutory architecture effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Under OBBBA Section 70302(a), Congress added IRC Section 174A, which restores default immediate expensing under Section 174A(a) for domestic research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, while preserving an optional election under Section 174A(c) to capitalize and amortize domestic research expenditures ratably over a period of not less than 60 months beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realizes benefits. Simultaneously, OBBBA Section 70302(b)(1) amended IRC Section 174 so that, for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, mandatory capitalization under Section 174 applies exclusively to foreign research or experimental expenditures, which remain permanently subject to mandatory 15-year (180-month) ratable amortization under the mid-year convention. For unamortized domestic SRE balances capitalized during the 2022 through 2024 tax years under TCJA Section 174, OBBBA Section 70302(f)(2) permits taxpayers either to continue amortizing those balances over their remaining 5-year schedules or to elect catch-up acceleration—deducting the remaining unamortized domestic balance in full in the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 (2025) or ratably over the two-taxable-year period spanning 2025 and 2026.

The shift from elective immediate expensing to mandatory capitalization (across all domestic and foreign research in 2022–2024, and permanently for foreign research and elective domestic capitalization in 2025 and beyond) fundamentally alters corporate cash flow, federal taxable income computation, and tax accounting administration. Because the mid-year convention restricts first-year amortization to half of a single year's ratable share—yielding a 10.0% (1/10th) deduction in Year 1 for 5-year domestic research and a 3.33% (1/30th) deduction in Year 1 for 15-year foreign research—the capitalization mandate functions as an immediate tax liability acceleration mechanism. For a hypothetical taxpayer incurring $1,000,000 in domestic SRE expenditures during the mandatory capitalization period, first-year tax recovery drops from $1,000,000 (100.0%) under the pre-2022 (and post-2024 Section 174A(a)) expensing rules to $100,000 (10.0%) under the 5-year capitalization regime, generating an immediate $900,000 upward adjustment to Year 1 federal taxable income. For $1,000,000 in foreign SRE expenditures, first-year tax recovery drops to $33,333.33 (3.33%), generating an immediate $966,666.67 upward adjustment to Year 1 federal taxable income. Furthermore, adherence to the IRC Section 174 and Section 174A substantive qualification rules is not discretionary; it serves as a foundational statutory prerequisite for establishing and quantifying Qualified Research Expenditures (QREs) eligible for the separate Research and Experimentation Tax Credit under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A).

Beyond immediate liquidity compression, mandatory capitalization introduces three structural imperatives for corporate tax administration. First, transitioning between immediate deduction and capitalization/amortization under TCJA Section 174, amended Section 174, or new Section 174A constitutes a change in method of accounting under IRC Section 446 and Section 481. For TCJA Section 174, this required procedural compliance via an automatic accounting method change statement in lieu of Form 3115 for the first effective taxable year beginning after December 31, 2021, or a formal Form 3115 (Application for Change in Accounting Method) with a modified Section 481(a) adjustment for subsequent taxable years, alongside annual reporting on Part VI of Form 4562 (Depreciation and Amortization)—procedures subsequently expanded by IRS Revenue Procedures 2023-8, 2023-11, 2023-24, 2024-9, 2024-23, 2025-8, 2025-23, 2025-28, and 2026-32. Second, IRC Section 174(d) strictly prohibits the accelerated deduction or basis recovery of unamortized balances upon the disposition, retirement, or abandonment of the underlying research project or resulting property (including an explicit statutory prohibition on reducing the amount realized for dispositions after May 12, 2025, under OBBBA Section 70302(b)(1)(C)), creating persistent "stranded costs" in taxable asset dispositions. Third, the statutory broadening of Section 174(c)(3) and Section 174A(d)(3) to classify all software development costs as research or experimental expenditures—paired with the broader scope of Sections 174 and 174A relative to Section 41—compels enterprises to construct granular cost-segregation frameworks that reliably demarcate domestic versus foreign research activities and separate capitalizable research costs from immediately deductible ordinary and necessary business expenses under IRC Section 162.
Legislative Evolution and the Statutory Scope of IRC Section 174
Historical Baseline of the Pre-2022 Expensing Regime

Prior to the effective date of the TCJA amendments, IRC Section 174 afforded businesses substantial flexibility in accounting for research and experimental (R&E) costs. For taxable years beginning on or before December 31, 2021, taxpayers could elect to deduct R&E expenditures entirely in the current taxable year paid or incurred under former Section 174(a), elect to treat them as deferred expenses amortizable ratably over a period of not less than 60 months beginning with the month the taxpayer first realized benefits from the expenditures under former Section 174(b), elect 10-year ratable amortization under IRC Section 59(e) (enacted in 1986), or charge the costs to a capital account and recover them through depreciation if the resulting asset had a determinable useful life.

In United States statutory history, Congress originally enacted IRC Section 174—establishing the statutory right to immediately deduct research and experimental expenditures under Section 174(a) or defer and amortize them over at least 60 months under Section 174(b)—as part of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 (Public Law 83-591). Prior to 1954, the Internal Revenue Code of 1939 contained no specific provision governing R&E outlays, forcing taxpayers to navigate general capitalization principles under former Section 23(a)(1) (ordinary and necessary business expenses) and former Section 24(a)(2) (capital items and permanent improvements), which left taxpayers with no means of amortizing capitalized research expenditures when a project was not abandoned and lacked a determinable useful life. Congress enacted Section 174 in 1954 specifically to eliminate that uncertainty and encourage research investment. By contrast, the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (ERTA, Public Law 97-34, Section 221(a), 95 Stat. 172, 241) introduced the separate incremental Research and Experimentation Tax Credit (originally codified at IRC Section 44F and subsequently redesignated as IRC Section 41) to provide a credit incentive atop Section 174 expensing.
The TCJA Revenue Raiser and Legislative Repeal Efforts

The elimination of elective expensing in favor of mandatory capitalization originated in Section 13206 of the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (P.L. 115-97), where Congress utilized the five-year delayed implementation of amended IRC Section 174 (effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021) as a primary budgetary "revenue raiser" to offset the fiscal cost of corporate and individual tax rate reductions within the broader budget reconciliation package. Because the amortization deferral shifted substantial corporate tax deductions out of the initial years of the ten-year Congressional budget window, the provision generated large near-term federal revenue increases on paper while imposing acute cash-tax increases on R&D-intensive enterprises beginning in the 2022 tax year.

Following the December 31, 2021 effective date, bipartisan legislative initiatives repeatedly sought to defer or repeal the mandatory domestic capitalization requirement during the 2022 through 2024 compliance cycles, most notably through H.R. 7024 (the Tax Relief for American Families and Workers Act of 2024), which proposed retroactively delaying mandatory domestic R&D capitalization. However, H.R. 7024 failed to achieve enactment during the 118th Congress, leaving mandatory TCJA Section 174 capitalization fully in force for both domestic and foreign SRE expenditures across the 2022, 2023, and 2024 tax years.

During the 119th Congress, the legislative impasse was resolved prospectively through the enactment of the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, Public Law 119-21, 139 Stat. 72), signed into law on July 4, 2025. Rather than repealing Section 174 in its entirety, Section 70302 of the OBBBA restructured the statutory framework into two parallel Code provisions effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, accompanied by transitional recovery elections for 2022–2024 domestic balances:

items: New IRC Section 174A for Domestic Research (Post-2024): OBBBA Section 70302(a) added IRC Section 174A, which restores immediate deductibility under Section 174A(a) for domestic research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Taxpayers that prefer to capitalize domestic research—for example, to manage Adjusted Taxable Income under IRC Section 163(j) or international tax calculations under BEAT and FDII/FDDEI—may elect under Section 174A(c) to charge domestic R&E expenditures to a capital account and amortize them ratably over a period of not less than 60 months beginning with the month the taxpayer first realizes benefits from the expenditures.

Amended IRC Section 174 for Foreign Research (Post-2024): OBBBA Section 70302(b)(1) amended IRC Section 174 to narrow its prospective scope exclusively to foreign research or experimental expenditures (attributable to research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States within the meaning of IRC Section 41(d)(4)(F)). Consequently, foreign R&E expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, remain permanently bound by the mandatory capitalization and 15-year (180-month) ratable amortization mandate under the mid-year convention.

Transition Rules for 2022–2024 Capitalized Domestic SRE Balances (OBBBA Section 70302(f)): For domestic SRE expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, mandatory capitalization under TCJA Section 174 remains the default rule under which taxpayers continue amortizing previously capitalized amounts over the remainder of their 5-year schedules. However, OBBBA Section 70302(f)(2) permits any taxpayer to elect catch-up acceleration—deducting the remaining unamortized amount of 2022–2024 domestic TCJA Section 174 expenditures either in full in its first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 (2025) or ratably over the two-taxable-year period beginning with that year (2025 and 2026). Additionally, OBBBA Section 70302(f) granted eligible small business taxpayers—defined under IRC Section 448(c) as taxpayers with average annual gross receipts of $31,000,000 or less over the three prior taxable years measured from 2025 (2022 through 2024) that are not tax shelters—a time-limited option to apply Section 174A retroactively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, via amended returns, Administrative Adjustment Requests (AARs), or an accounting method change under Revenue Procedure 2025-28 filed on or before the earlier of July 6, 2026, or the expiration of the statute of limitations for credit or refund under IRC Section 6511.

body.text: Defining Specified Research or Experimental Expenditures and Software Inclusion

Under TCJA-amended IRC Section 174(b) (and mirrored in post-2024 Section 174(b) for foreign research and Section 174A(b) for domestic research), "specified research or experimental expenditures" (and domestic/foreign R&E expenditures) encompass expenditures paid or incurred during the taxable year in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business that represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense. As codified in Treasury Regulation Section 1.174-2(a)(1) and reaffirmed in Section 4.02 of IRS Notice 2023-63, this standard captures activities intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement or appropriate design of a product, process, formula, invention, technique, patent, or similar property (or a component or subcomponent thereof). Furthermore, Treasury Regulation Section 1.174-2(a)(9) stipulates that Section 174 applies to a research or experimental expenditure only to the extent that the amount of the expenditure is reasonable under the circumstances—defined generally as the amount that would ordinarily be paid for like activities by like enterprises under like circumstances.

A transformative and permanent provision of the statutory regime is IRC Section 174(c)(3) (and parallel IRC Section 174A(d)(3) enacted by the OBBBA), which explicitly mandates that any amount paid or incurred in connection with the development of any software shall be treated as a specified research or experimental expenditure (or domestic/foreign R&E expenditure). Prior to 2022, taxpayers frequently relied on the administrative safe harbor of Revenue Procedure 2000-50 (2000-2 C.B. 601), which permitted the immediate deduction of software development costs consistently treated as current expenses (or ratable amortization over 60 months from completion or 36 months from the date placed in service), independent of whether those software development activities satisfied the strict technological uncertainty definition of research under Treasury Regulation Section 1.174-2. By bringing all software development squarely inside Section 174(c)(3) and Section 174A(d)(3), the statute abolished the separate accounting flexibility of Revenue Procedure 2000-50 for post-2021 tax years. Specifically, Section 12 of IRS Notice 2023-63, as clarified by Section 5 of Notice 2024-12 and Revenue Procedure 2024-9, formally removed Section 5 of Revenue Procedure 2000-50 as obsolete for software development expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, while confirming that Section 5 of Revenue Procedure 2000-50 continues to apply to amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning on or before December 31, 2021. Consequently, technology firms, financial institutions, and industrial enterprises investing in proprietary, commercial, or internal-use software development were required to capitalize those expenditures and amortize them over 5 years (if developed domestically) or 15 years (if developed abroad) during 2022–2024, and from 2025 onward must continue capitalizing and amortizing all foreign software development over 15 years under Section 174 while treating domestic software development as an R&E expenditure under Section 174A.

Under Section 5 of IRS Notice 2023-63, computer software is defined broadly as any computer program or routine (and any sequence of code) designed to cause a computer to perform a desired function or set of functions, and the documentation required to describe and maintain that program or routine, including code stored on computing devices, affixed to physical media, or accessed remotely via cloud computing, encompassing system software, programming software, application software, and embedded software. Capitalizable software development activities under Notice 2023-63 include planning the development of computer software (including identification and documentation of software requirements), designing the computer software (or upgrades and enhancements that result in additional functionality or materially increase speed or efficiency), building a model, writing source code and converting it to machine-readable code, and testing and making necessary modifications up until the software is placed in service (for internal-use software) or ready for sale or licensing to others (for commercial software). Conversely, Section 5.05 of Notice 2023-63 excludes employee training, post-placement maintenance activities that do not give rise to upgrades and enhancements (such as corrective maintenance to debug, diagnose, and fix programming errors), data conversion activities (other than developing software to facilitate data conversion), installation activities, and post-readiness marketing and promotional activities.

Furthermore, IRC Section 174(c)(1)–(2) (and parallel IRC Section 174A(d)(1)–(2)) establishes explicit statutory exclusions from SRE and R&E treatment. Specifically, qualifying research expenditures exclude any expenditure for the acquisition or improvement of land, as well as any expenditure for the acquisition or improvement of property of a character subject to an allowance for depreciation under IRC Section 167 or depletion under IRC Section 611, even when that property is utilized directly in connection with research or experimentation. Crucially, however, while the capital acquisition cost of depreciable equipment or facilities is excluded from Sections 174 and 174A, the annual depreciation allowances under Section 167 and depletion allowances under Section 611 attributable to property used in the performance or direct support of research activities are treated as SRE/R&E expenditures subject to Section 174 capitalization and amortization (or Section 174A treatment). In addition, the statute explicitly excludes expenditures paid or incurred for the purpose of ascertaining the existence, location, extent, or quality of any deposit of ore or other mineral, including oil and gas (mineral exploration expenditures), from treatment as SRE or R&E expenditures.
Mechanics of Capitalization, Amortization Schedules, and Financial Modeling
Domestic Versus Foreign Recovery Periods and the Mid-Year Convention

The mechanics of cost recovery under TCJA IRC Section 174(a)(2)(B) (for 2022–2024) and OBBBA-amended Section 174(a)(2)(B) (for post-2024 foreign research) bifurcate strictly according to the geographic location where the research activities are performed. Under Section 3.04 of IRS Notice 2023-63, taxpayers must look to where the specific research activities are performed to determine whether the corresponding expenditures are attributable to domestic or foreign research. SRE expenditures attributable to domestic research (conducted within the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States) were required to be amortized ratably over a 5-year (60-month) period for taxable years beginning in 2022, 2023, and 2024 (and for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, are immediately deductible under Section 174A(a) unless the taxpayer elects amortization over at least 60 months under Section 174A(c) or elects 1-year or 2-year transition recovery of unamortized 2022–2024 balances under OBBBA Section 70302(f)(2)). Conversely, expenditures attributable to foreign research (conducted outside the United States, Puerto Rico, and U.S. possessions within the meaning of IRC Section 41(d)(4)(F)) must be capitalized and amortized ratably over a 15-year (180-month) period under both TCJA Section 174 and OBBBA-amended Section 174. This three-fold extension of the amortization horizon for offshore research during 2022–2024—and the permanent divergence between immediate domestic expensing under Section 174A(a) and 15-year foreign amortization under Section 174 from 2025 onward—creates an intentional statutory penalty on foreign R&D outsourcing and offshoring, strongly favoring domestic research localization.

Both the 5-year domestic schedule and the 15-year foreign schedule under Section 174(a)(2)(B) are governed by a mandatory midpoint convention: amortization begins at the midpoint of the taxable year in which the SRE expenditures are paid or incurred. Under a standard twelve-month taxable year, the mid-year convention treats all SRE expenditures incurred at any point during the year—whether in January or December—as having been placed into the amortization pool exactly halfway through the year (generating 6 months of amortization in Year 1). (For short taxable years, Section 3.06 of Notice 2023-63 provides specific midpoint rules based on the number of months in the short taxable year.)

Mathematically, for a total SRE expenditure E amortized over N years (12 × N months) under a standard twelve-month taxable year mid-year convention, the annual amortization deduction A<sub>t</sub> in taxable year t (where t = 1, 2, ..., N + 1) is defined by:
A<sub>t</sub> = E / (2N) for t = 1 and t = N + 1; A<sub>t</sub> = E / N for t = 2, ..., N

For 5-year domestic research (N = 5), the full annual ratable rate is 20.0% (1/5), but the mid-year convention restricts the Year 1 deduction to 10.0% (1/10), followed by 20.0% (1/5) annually in Years 2 through 5, and a final 10.0% (1/10) deduction in Year 6 (10.0% + 20.0% + 20.0% + 20.0% + 20.0% + 10.0% = 100.0%). For 15-year foreign research (N = 15), the full annual ratable rate is 6.67% (1/15), while the mid-year convention restricts the Year 1 deduction to 3.33% (1/30), followed by 6.67% (1/15) annually in Years 2 through 15 (14 full years), and a final 3.33% (1/30) deduction in Year 16 (1/30 + 14/15 + 1/30 = 100.0%). Thus, recovering a single year's research cohort under Section 174 requires 6 distinct tax years for 5-year domestic activities and 16 distinct tax years for 15-year foreign activities.
Hypothetical Worked Example: Cash Flow and Taxable Income Impact

To demonstrate the exact quantitative impact of the capitalization mandate, consider a hypothetical United States corporation that incurs $1,000,000 in qualifying domestic SRE expenditures (or, for comparison, $1,000,000 in foreign SRE expenditures) during Year 1. Under the pre-2022 immediate expensing rules (and under post-2024 Section 174A(a) domestic expensing rules), the taxpayer deducted the entire $1,000,000 (100.0%) in Year 1, reducing Year 1 federal taxable income by the full $1,000,000 expenditure amount and leaving $0 of remaining tax basis for subsequent years.

Under the post-2021 mandatory capitalization regime (applicable to 2022–2024 domestic cohorts absent a transition acceleration election), the same hypothetical $1,000,000 domestic outlay must be capitalized and amortized over 5 years using the mid-year convention. In Year 1, the taxpayer may deduct only $100,000 (10.0%), resulting in an immediate $900,000 reduction in tax deductions—and an equivalent +$900,000 increase in federal taxable income—relative to immediate expensing. In Years 2, 3, 4, and 5, the taxpayer deducts $200,000 (20.0%) per year, and in Year 6, the remaining $100,000 (10.0%) is deducted. If the hypothetical $1,000,000 expenditure is instead incurred for foreign research (in any tax year from 2022 onward), the Year 1 deduction is limited to $33,333.33 (3.33%, or 1/30th), deferring $966,666.67 of the deduction into Years 2 through 16 ($66,666.67 per year in Years 2 through 15, and $33,333.33 in Year 16).

body.text: Although the nominal cumulative deduction over the 6-year domestic window (or 16-year foreign window) ultimately equals $1,000,000, the severe front-loaded deferral extracts working capital from innovative businesses in the initial years of transition. Evaluation of multi-year R&D spending patterns indicates that for a business maintaining a constant $1,000,000 annual R&D budget under the 5-year mid-year schedule, the stacking of overlapping amortization layers yields aggregate deductions of $100,000 (10.0%) in Year 1, $300,000 (30.0%) in Year 2, $500,000 (50.0%) in Year 3, $700,000 (70.0%) in Year 4, $900,000 (90.0%) in Year 5, and $1,000,000 (100.0%) in Year 6—requiring five full years of domestic R&D cohorts (reaching Year 6 of the initial cohort) before annual aggregate amortization deductions converge back toward the annual cash R&D outlay. Furthermore, for a taxpayer that capitalized $1,000,000 per year of domestic SRE expenditures in 2022, 2023, and 2024 ($3,000,000 cumulative spend, with $100,000 deducted in 2022, $300,000 in 2023, and $500,000 in 2024), the remaining unamortized domestic balance entering 2025 is $2,100,000 ($500,000 from 2022, $700,000 from 2023, and $900,000 from 2024), which under OBBBA Section 70302(f)(2) may be deducted in full ($2,100,000) in 2025 or ratably ($1,050,000 per year) across 2025 and 2026.
Intersection of IRC Section 174 Capitalization with the IRC Section 41 R&D Tax Credit
Statutory Hierarchy: Why Section 174 Is Broader Than Section 41

A critical compliance requirement under federal tax law is the statutory linkage between IRC Section 174 (and post-2024 IRC Section 174A) and the IRC Section 41 Credit for Increasing Research Activities (commonly referred to as the R&D Tax Credit). To qualify as "qualified research" under IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A), an activity must first represent research with respect to which expenditures may be treated as specified research or experimental expenditures under IRC Section 174 (for taxable years beginning in 2022–2024) or as domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC Section 174A (for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, following the OBBBA conforming amendment to Section 41(d)(1)). Consequently, categorizing and properly accounting for a cost under Section 174 (or Section 174A) is an absolute statutory prerequisite before that expenditure can be included as a Qualified Research Expenditure (QRE) in the Section 41 credit computation. Moreover, Section 4.02(3) of IRS Notice 2023-63 establishes a strict consistency mandate: SRE expenditures must be treated consistently for purposes of all provisions under Subtitle A of the Internal Revenue Code.

However, the relationship between Sections 174/174A and Section 41 is asymmetrical: while every Section 41 QRE must satisfy Section 174 or Section 174A, not every Section 174 SRE expenditure or Section 174A R&E expenditure qualifies as a Section 41 QRE. Section 41 restricts QREs to narrow categories of direct domestic research inputs—specifically in-house research wages for qualified services, supplies used and consumed directly in conducting qualified research, computer leasing or cloud hosting payments for computers used directly in qualified research, and 65% (or applicable statutory percentages) of contract research expenses—and further requires that the expenditures be incurred "in carrying on" a trade or business (a stricter threshold than Section 174's "in connection with" a trade or business standard) while satisfying the technological-in-nature and process-of-experimentation tests.

In contrast, Sections 174 and 174A capture the comprehensive pool of direct and allocable indirect costs incident to the development or improvement of a product, process, or software in the experimental or laboratory sense. As detailed in Section 4.03 of IRS Notice 2023-63, Section 174 SRE expenditures include labor costs for full-time, part-time, and contract employees and independent contractors who perform, supervise, or directly support SRE activities (encompassing basic compensation, stock-based compensation, overtime, vacation, holiday, and sick pay, payroll taxes, pension costs, and employee benefits, while explicitly excluding severance compensation), materials and supplies (including nondepreciable tools and equipment), cost recovery allowances (depreciation, amortization, or depletion under Sections 167 and 611 on property used in performing or directly supporting SRE activities), patent procurement costs (including attorney's fees incurred in making and perfecting a patent application), allocable facility and overhead expenses (rent, utilities, insurance, taxes, repairs, and security for R&D facilities), and travel costs for performing or directly supporting SRE activities. Patent procurement costs, indirect facility overhead, equipment depreciation allowances, and foreign research activities must all be accounted for under Section 174 (or Section 174A), yet all of those categories are excluded from QRE eligibility under Section 41. Conversely, Section 4.03(2) of Notice 2023-63 confirms that costs paid or incurred by general and administrative (G&A) service departments or functions that only indirectly support or benefit SRE activities (such as payroll, human resources, and accounting departments), interest on debt to finance SRE activities, website content input costs, website hosting fees, domain name/trademark registration costs, and costs listed in Treasury Regulation Section 1.174-2(a)(6)(i)–(vii) are neither permitted nor required to be treated as SRE expenditures.

In addition, taxpayers claiming the Section 41 credit must apply IRC Section 280C(c). Under TCJA Section 13206(d)(2)(A) (effective for 2022–2024), IRC Section 280C(c)(1) provided that if the Section 41 research credit for the taxable year exceeded the amount allowable as a deduction for qualified research expenses or basic research expenses for that taxable year, the amount chargeable to the Section 174 capital account for such expenses had to be reduced by the amount of that excess, unless the taxpayer elected the reduced research credit under Section 280C(c)(2). Under OBBBA Section 70302(b)(2)(B) (effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, with no inference for pre-2025 taxable years under OBBBA Section 70302(e)(4)), amended IRC Section 280C(c)(1) requires that domestic R&E expenditures otherwise deductible under Section 174A(a) or chargeable to a capital account under Section 174A(c) be reduced directly by the amount of the Section 41(a) research credit allowed, unless the taxpayer makes a timely reduced credit election under Section 280C(c)(2).
Dual Tracking Requirements and Expanded Cost Segregation

Prior to the 2022 effective date of mandatory capitalization, taxpayers claiming the Section 41 credit frequently focused their documentation and cost-tracking workflows exclusively on direct QRE categories (wages, supplies, and contract research). Because non-QRE research costs (such as R&D facility overhead, utilities, depreciation allowances on research equipment, quality control testing in the experimental phase, and patent legal fees) were immediately deductible regardless of whether they were classified as Section 174 R&E expenses or Section 162 ordinary and necessary business expenses, taxpayers rarely maintained separate accounting ledgers for non-creditable Section 174 expenses.

Under the post-2021 statutory regime, this historical accounting shortcut creates substantial audit exposure. Even if a taxpayer elects not to claim the Section 41 R&D Tax Credit—or incurs indirect R&D costs or foreign research outlays that are ineligible for the Section 41 credit—the taxpayer is legally required to identify, segregate, and properly account for all Section 174 SRE expenditures (and post-2024 Section 174 foreign and Section 174A domestic expenditures). This mandate necessitates dual-tracking accounting architectures capable of capturing both the broad perimeter of direct and allocable indirect costs governed by Section 174 and Section 174A (strictly separated between domestic and foreign performance locations) and the narrower subset of direct domestic costs eligible for the tax credit under Section 41.

Credit calculation is unaffected by subsequent abandonment, provided costs were validly paid or incurred in the credit year.

body.text: Advanced Strategic, Transactional, and Accounting Implications
Dispositions, Retirements, and Abandonments Under IRC Section 174(d)

Among the most consequential structural provisions introduced by the TCJA amendments—and permanently reinforced for foreign research by the OBBBA—is IRC Section 174(d), which governs the disposition, retirement, or abandonment of property with respect to which SRE (or foreign R&E) expenditures have been paid or incurred. Under general federal income tax principles (such as IRC Section 165 and Section 1001), when a taxpayer abandons an unsuccessful capital project, retires an obsolete asset, or disposes of property in a taxable sale, the remaining unrecovered tax basis may typically be written off immediately as an abandonment loss or subtracted from the amount realized to compute gain or loss. Section 174(d) explicitly overrides this principle for capitalized research expenditures, mandating that if any property with respect to which SRE expenditures are paid or incurred is disposed of, retired, or abandoned during the 5-year or 15-year amortization period, no deduction shall be allowed with respect to such expenditures on account of such disposition, retirement, or abandonment, and the amortization deduction must continue over the remaining statutory period. Furthermore, OBBBA Section 70302(b)(1)(C) and Section 70302(e)(2)(A) amended IRC Section 174(d) for property disposed of, retired, or abandoned after May 12, 2025, to specify explicitly in the statutory text that "no deduction or reduction to amount realized" is permitted on account of such disposition, retirement, or abandonment, while OBBBA updated IRC Section 1016(a)(14) to reference Sections 174 and 174A(c). Equivalently, in a taxable sale of the property, the unamortized Section 174 balance cannot be used as asset basis under IRC Section 1001 or Section 1060(c) to reduce the amount realized or decrease taxable gain on the sale.

This statutory prohibition creates severe distortions—referred to in corporate tax practice as "stranded costs"—during mergers, acquisitions, and corporate restructurings. In taxable asset dispositions and other non-Section 381 transactions (such as a taxable sale of assets under IRC Section 1001 or Section 1060(c), or a transfer of property in an IRC Section 351 exchange where the transferor corporation remains in existence), Section 7.02 of IRS Notice 2023-63 confirms that Section 174(d) prevents the selling or transferring corporation from applying its unamortized SRE balance against the sale proceeds to reduce taxable gain. Instead, the selling corporation recognizes full gain on the disposition while retaining the "stranded" unamortized SRE asset on its own tax books, recovering those deductions gradually over the remaining 5- or 15-year statutory period, while the acquiring party receives no tax basis or benefit from the seller's prior Section 174 schedule. Under Section 7.03 of Notice 2023-63, even if property is disposed of before the midpoint of the taxable year in which the SRE expenditures were paid or incurred, amortization still begins at the midpoint of that taxable year and continues over the full statutory recovery period.

Conversely, Section 7.04 of IRS Notice 2023-63 outlines two distinct rules when a corporation ceases to exist for federal income tax purposes. First, under Section 7.04(1) of Notice 2023-63, the primary exception where unamortized SRE schedules transfer to a successor entity occurs in corporate cessation transactions governed by IRC Section 381(a), such as complete subsidiary liquidations under IRC Section 332 or qualifying tax-free corporate reorganizations. In transactions where Section 381(a) applies, the acquiring transferee corporation "steps into the shoes" of the distributor or transferor corporation and continues amortizing the remaining SRE balance over the remainder of the transferor's original recovery schedule. Second, under Section 7.04(2) of Notice 2023-63, if a corporation ceases to exist for federal income tax purposes in a transaction or series of transactions to which Section 381(a) does not apply (such as a taxable complete liquidation), the corporation is allowed a deduction equal to its unamortized SRE expenditures in its final taxable year, subject to an anti-abuse exception if a principal purpose of the transaction was to claim the deduction or accelerate recovery of unamortized SRE expenditures. However, Section 10.01 of Notice 2023-63 (as modified by Section 4 of Notice 2024-12) expressly prohibits taxpayers from relying on the rules of Section 7 of Notice 2023-63 for SRE expenditures paid or incurred with respect to property contributed to, distributed from, or transferred from a partnership. This framework compels M&A due diligence teams to track SRE pools at the project and legal-entity level prior to structuring transactions.
Cascading Effects Across Federal, International, and State Tax Provisions

Because mandatory capitalization under Section 174 (and conversely, immediate expensing under post-2024 Section 174A or catch-up acceleration of 2022–2024 domestic balances under OBBBA Section 70302(f)(2)) alters near-term federal taxable income before special deductions, it triggers second- and third-order ripple effects across interconnected provisions of the Internal Revenue Code and state tax regimes. Within the domestic corporate tax computation, a higher initial measure of federal taxable income before the deduction of business interest directly impacts the limitation on business interest expense under IRC Section 163(j). Because deductible business interest under Section 163(j) is capped as a percentage of Adjusted Taxable Income (ATI), the deferral of R&D deductions under Section 174 (or an affirmative election to capitalize and amortize domestic R&E over at least 60 months under Section 174A(c)) increases a taxpayer's initial taxable income base and ATI, which can yield a higher interest deduction ceiling for leveraged enterprises, as well as affecting charitable contribution limits under IRC Section 170 and the Corporate Alternative Minimum Tax (CAMT).

Simultaneously, changes to domestic and foreign research cost recovery alter the underlying tax base and expense allocations (such as under IRC Section 864) used in computing international tax provisions, requiring meticulous financial modeling across the Base Erosion and Anti-Abuse Tax (BEAT, IRC Section 59A), Global Intangible Low-Taxed Income (GILTI, IRC Section 951A), and Foreign-Derived Intangible Income / Foreign-Derived Deduction Eligible Income (FDII / FDDEI, IRC Section 250). In addition, Section 6 of IRS Notice 2023-63 (as clarified by Notice 2024-12) establishes a "risks and rights" test for research performed under contract: a contract research provider's costs are subject to Section 174 capitalization only if the provider (i) contractually bears the financial risk of loss related to failure to produce the desired product, or (ii) acquires a right to use any resulting SRE product in its trade or business or otherwise exploit it through sale, lease, or license (excluding rights separately bargained for or acquired solely for the limited purpose of performing SRE activities under contract with the research recipient). Consequently, when a U.S. company hires a foreign affiliate to perform contract research under an R&D service agreement where the foreign affiliate bears no financial risk and retains no exploitation rights, Section 174 does not apply to the foreign affiliate's costs—allowing the foreign affiliate to deduct its operating expenses currently under IRC Section 162 for purposes of computing Subpart F income and GILTI tested income—while the U.S. parent (the research recipient and IP owner) capitalizes and amortizes the contract payments over 15 years under Section 174 and Treasury Regulation Section 1.174-2(a)(10) and (b)(3). Notice 2023-63 also clarifies that under Treasury Regulation Section 1.482-7(j)(3)(i), Cost Sharing Transaction (CST) payments owed to a controlled participant in a cost-sharing arrangement reduce the amount of intangible development costs borne directly by that participant that are required to be charged to the Section 174 capital account.

Beyond the federal return, corporate taxpayers must manage substantial compliance divergence at the state level. While "rolling conformity" states (such as Delaware, the District of Columbia, and Illinois) automatically adopt the Internal Revenue Code as currently amended—imposing mandatory Section 174 capitalization during 2022–2024 and automatically adopting OBBBA Section 174A domestic expensing for 2025 onward unless state decoupling thresholds apply, such as Maryland's automatic decoupling rule when the revenue impact is $5,000,000 or more—static conformity and explicitly decoupled states require separate state-level R&D tracking and modification schedules. Specifically, several major states decoupled from TCJA Section 174 mandatory capitalization and continued to allow immediate R&E expensing throughout 2022–2024, including California (which generally conforms to the IRC as of January 1, 2015), Georgia (via S.B. 56, enacted May 2, 2023, applying Section 174 as in effect prior to the TCJA), Indiana (via S.B. 419, enacted May 4, 2023), Tennessee (following Section 174 as it existed on December 31, 2017), Wisconsin (adopting the pre-TCJA version of Section 174), and Alabama (decoupling effective January 1, 2024, to follow 2021 IRC Section 174). In those decoupled states, taxpayers that deducted 100% of domestic R&E on their 2022–2024 state returns must make state addition modifications in 2025 and 2026 to avoid duplicative state deductions when claiming federal catch-up amortization under OBBBA Section 70302(f)(2). Conversely, static conformity states whose fixed IRC conformity date is anchored to the Code as in effect during 2022–2024 (such as Florida, Hawaii, and North Carolina prior to legislative conformity updates) continue to require 5-year state-level domestic Section 174 amortization unless and until state legislation advances their IRC conformity dates to adopt P.L. 119-21. Furthermore, because not all states conform to federal IRC Section 280C(c), taxpayers must separately evaluate state subtraction modifications where Section 280C(c) reduced federal R&E deductions or capital accounts.
Financial Statement Accounting: ASC 730 Versus IRC Section 174

The divergence between U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) and federal tax law under Section 174 (and elective Section 174A(c)) generates substantial book-tax accounting differences governed by Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) Accounting Standards Codification (ASC) Topic 730 (Research and Development) and ASC Topic 740 (Income Taxes). Under U.S. GAAP—specifically ASC 730-10-25-1—costs incurred for research and development activities are generally required to be expensed immediately on the financial statement income statement in the period incurred.

Because a company expenses 100.0% of R&D costs immediately for GAAP book purposes under ASC 730-10-25-1 while capitalizing 90.0% of domestic SRE costs (deducting 10.0% in Year 1 under the 5-year mid-year schedule) or 96.67% of foreign SRE costs (deducting 3.33% in Year 1 under the 15-year mid-year schedule) in Year 1 for tax purposes under IRC Section 174, a deductible temporary book-tax difference arises. Under ASC 740, this temporary difference requires the recognition of a Deferred Tax Asset (DTA) on the financial statement balance sheet, representing the future tax benefit of the amortization deductions that will reverse over the remaining 5- or 15-year statutory period. Management teams and external auditors must carefully evaluate the likelihood of generating sufficient future taxable income to realize these deferred tax benefits and assess whether a valuation allowance must be established against the Section 174 DTAs under ASC 740, a determination that directly affects the Effective Tax Rate (ETR) reported on audited financial statements.
Regulatory Compliance and IRS Administrative Procedures
Accounting Method Changes Under IRC Section 446 and Modified Section 481(a) Rules

Under the statutory transition rules of TCJA Section 13206(b) and OBBBA Section 70302(c), the shift between immediate expensing and capitalization/amortization under TCJA Section 174, amended Section 174, or new Section 174A is treated as a mandatory or elective change in method of accounting under IRC Section 446(e) and Section 481 initiated by the taxpayer and made with the consent of the Secretary. Crucially, TCJA Section 13206(b) and IRS procedural guidance mandated that the initial transition to TCJA Section 174 be implemented on a cut-off basis for the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2021.

Under this cut-off rule, the accounting method change applies exclusively to SRE expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, meaning that pre-2022 R&E expenditures retain their prior tax treatment and are not retroactively capitalized. For a taxpayer that implemented the TCJA Section 174 accounting method change in a taxable year subsequent to its first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2021, the transition requires computing a modified Section 481(a) adjustment that takes into account only SRE expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, avoiding any cumulative adjustment reaching back into pre-change (pre-2022) years. Furthermore, under Section 7.02(7) of Revenue Procedure 2023-24 (and Revenue Procedure 2024-9), taxpayers receive only limited audit protection: audit protection does not apply for expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning on or before December 31, 2021, nor does audit protection apply for post-2021 expenditures if the method change is made for the taxable year immediately subsequent to the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2021.

Similarly, under OBBBA Section 70302(c)(1) and Revenue Procedure 2025-28, changes to comply with new IRC Section 174A for domestic R&E expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, are treated as initiated by the taxpayer, made with the Commissioner's automatic consent, and applied strictly on a cut-off basis with no Section 481(a) adjustment for post-2024 expenditures. Separate automatic method change rules under OBBBA Section 70302(f)(2), Revenue Procedure 2025-28, and Revenue Procedure 2026-32 govern the 1-year (2025) or 2-year (2025–2026) recovery of remaining unamortized 2022–2024 domestic TCJA Section 174 amounts (and coordinate any concurrent net positive Section 481(a) adjustment from a late TCJA Section 174 method change so that it is taken into account over the same 1-year or 2-year recovery period elected by the taxpayer).
Procedural Filing Rules: Revenue Procedures 2023-8 and 2023-24 and Form 4562

The Internal Revenue Service established and iteratively refined the automatic consent procedures for adopting post-2021 Section 174 capitalization and post-2024 Section 174A / amended Section 174 rules across a comprehensive series of administrative guidance documents. Initially, the IRS issued Revenue Procedure 2023-8 (December 12, 2022), which was modified and superseded by Revenue Procedure 2023-11 (December 29, 2022, adding a transition rule deeming taxpayers that filed a post-2021 return on or before January 17, 2023, and properly reported SRE amortization on Form 4562 to have complied with Section 446 method change procedures), and subsequently incorporated into Section 7.02 of Revenue Procedure 2023-24 (June 2023) under Designated Automatic Accounting Method Change Number (DCN) 265.

In September 2023, the Treasury Department and IRS released substantive interim guidance in Notice 2023-63 (effective for taxable years ending after September 8, 2023, with early adoption permitted) to clarify the identification and allocation of SRE expenditures, software development, contract research, Section 174(d) dispositions, cost-sharing arrangements under IRC Section 482, and long-term contracts under IRC Section 460. In December 2023, the IRS issued Notice 2024-12 (modifying Notice 2023-63 to clarify contract research excluded product rights, eliminate the requirement that taxpayers relying on any rule in Notice 2023-63 must rely on all rules in Sections 3 through 9, and clarify that Section 5 of Revenue Procedure 2000-50 was obsoleted only for post-2021 taxable years) alongside Revenue Procedure 2024-9 (modifying Sections 7, 9, and 19 of Revenue Procedure 2023-24 to establish DCN 270 for relying on Notice 2023-63/2024-12 and adding Section 19.02 to allow Percentage-of-Completion Method taxpayers under IRC Section 460 to include only the current year's Section 174 amortization deduction rather than the full capitalized SRE amount in computing contract completion). Subsequent annual automatic change updates in Revenue Procedure 2024-23 (April 30, 2024), Revenue Procedure 2025-8 (December 17, 2024), and Revenue Procedure 2025-23 consolidated TCJA Section 174 changes under Section 7.01 (DCN 265).

Following the July 4, 2025 enactment of the OBBBA (P.L. 119-21), the IRS issued Revenue Procedure 2025-28 (effective August 28, 2025) and Revenue Procedure 2026-32 (issued in September 2026 and effective for Forms 3115 filed after September 4, 2026, with a transition option for duplicate Forms 3115 filed on or before November 15, 2026), modifying Section 7 of Revenue Procedure 2025-23 across three designated change numbers: DCN 265 (Section 7.01, for pre-2025 domestic TCJA Section 174 changes), DCN 273 (Section 7.02, for post-2024 domestic Section 174A expensing or Section 174A(c) capitalization elections and OBBBA Section 70302(f)(2) 1-year or 2-year recovery of unamortized 2022–2024 domestic TCJA Section 174 balances), and DCN 274 (Section 7.03, for foreign R&E expenditures under both TCJA Section 174 and post-2024 amended Section 174, removing the prior pre-2026 taxable year limitation and extending certain eligibility waivers to taxable years beginning before 2028).
The specific procedural filing requirements depend strictly on the taxable year and statutory provision under which the taxpayer implements the accounting method change:

cells: First Taxable Year Beginning After December 31, 2021 (Initial TCJA § 174 Adoption)
Rev. Proc. 2023-8; superseded by Rev. Proc. 2023-11 and Rev. Proc. 2023-24 (§ 7.02, DCN 265).
Simplified Statement in Lieu of Form 3115 attached to the original federal income tax return.
Applied strictly on a cut-off basis (applies only to SREs paid or incurred in that first post-2021 year).
Reported on Part VI (Amortization) of Form 4562, Depreciation and Amortization.
Subsequent Taxable Years Beginning After December 31, 2021, and Before January 1, 2025 (TCJA § 174 & Notice 2023-63)

Requires a modified IRC § 481(a) adjustment incorporating only SRE expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021.

body.text: Regardless of whether the accounting method change was perfected via the simplified statement in lieu of Form 3115 in the first effective year (or under the OBBBA transition procedures of Revenue Procedure 2025-28) or via a full Form 3115 in a subsequent year, ongoing annual compliance for all capitalized amounts requires reporting the current year's amortized deduction on Part VI of Form 4562 (Depreciation and Amortization) attached to the federal income tax return.
Operational Recommendations for Cost Segregation and Compliance

Because mandatory capitalization governed all domestic and foreign SRE expenditures during the 2022–2024 tax years and remains permanently in force for all foreign research under IRC Section 174 from 2025 onward—while domestic R&E requires navigating new IRC Section 174A, OBBBA transition recovery elections, Section 280C(c) reductions, and state non-conformity—corporate tax departments and financial controllers must maintain defensible cost segregation and compliance processes. The central operational challenge facing taxpayers is establishing a reliable demarcation along both geographic lines (domestic Section 174A versus foreign Section 174) and functional lines (research expenditures under Sections 174/174A versus routine costs that remain immediately deductible as ordinary and necessary business expenses under IRC Section 162). Historically, because pre-2022 law permitted immediate deductions under both Section 174 and Section 162 regardless of location, taxpayers rarely maintained rigorous accounting boundaries between Section 174, Section 174A, and Section 162 outlays.
To mitigate examination exposure and ensure accurate compliance, corporate tax leadership should execute four integrated operational initiatives:

items: Jurisdictional and Functional Cost Segregation: First, enterprises must refine their internal cost-classification and project-tracking systems to segregate domestic research activities under Section 174A from foreign research activities subject to mandatory 15-year amortization under Section 174, while simultaneously separating costs meeting the Section 174/174A standard of research "in the experimental or laboratory sense" (including software development under Section 174(c)(3) and Section 174A(d)(3)) from routine operational, maintenance, quality assurance, and general administrative expenses deductible under Section 162. In software development environments, working with engineering and accounting teams to separate genuine developmental innovation, initial code writing, and functional upgrades/enhancements (governed by Sections 174(c)(3) and 174A(d)(3)) from post-release corrective maintenance, debugging, employee training, and installation (expensed under Section 162 per Section 5.05 of Notice 2023-63) directly prevents unnecessary capitalization of offshore software maintenance and accurately scopes domestic R&E pools.

Defensible Indirect Cost Allocation and G&A Exclusion Methodologies: Second, given historical regulatory ambiguity regarding indirect research costs, taxpayers must model, formalize, and document defensible allocation methodologies for shared indirect costs—such as facility rent, utilities, and equipment depreciation allowances under Section 167 that directly support the R&D function—while systematically excluding indirect general and administrative (G&A) service department expenses (payroll, HR, and accounting), severance pay, and debt interest under Section 4.03(2) of IRS Notice 2023-63 so that contemporaneous workpapers substantiate the tax return positions upon IRS examination.

Proactive Alignment with IRS Administrative Guidance and OBBBA Modeling: Third, tax departments must proactively apply IRS Notice 2023-63, Notice 2024-12, Revenue Procedure 2025-28, and Revenue Procedure 2026-32 to model the optimal interaction between current domestic expensing under Section 174A(a), elective 60-month capitalization under Section 174A(c), and 1-year (2025) versus 2-year (2025–2026) transition recovery of unamortized 2022–2024 domestic TCJA Section 174 balances across IRC Section 163(j), BEAT, GILTI, FDII/FDDEI, CAMT, Section 280C(c), and state non-conformity adjustments.

Procedural Audit of Accounting Method Change Filings and Form 4562 Reconciliations: Fourth, taxpayers must conduct a comprehensive procedural review of their post-2021 federal returns to verify that all required accounting method changes under DCNs 265, 270, 273, and 274 were timely perfected—either through the statement in lieu of Form 3115 or via a formal Form 3115 under Revenue Procedures 2023-24, 2024-9, 2025-23, 2025-28, and 2026-32 (including observing the November 15, 2026 transition deadline in Revenue Procedure 2026-32)—and that annual amortization deductions are accurately reconciled to Part VI of Form 4562.
